title: Docs Plan: Workload-aware batching profiles (fast / standard / cost-efficient)
author: Elliot Price
body:
## Summary
This page outlines the documentation work required to launch and support **workload-aware batching profiles** (“batching tiers”) across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments. The feature introduces a customer-facing `batching_tier` selector with three options:
- `fast`
- `standard`
- `cost_efficient`

Docs must clearly explain:
1) what the tiers do (trade-offs, when to choose each),
2) how to configure tiers and overrides (precedence rules),
3) how to validate the effective runtime behavior (telemetry, headers, Console), and
4) how to migrate safely from explicit batching knobs.

The goal is to reduce support load and ensure customers make correct choices for latency SLOs, streaming cadence, and cost optimization.

## Target audience
Primary
- Application developers integrating Redwood inference (API + SDK users)
- ML/platform engineers who tune latency/cost and capacity

Secondary
- Solutions Engineering and Support (troubleshooting + enablement)
- SRE/Infra partners (rollout monitoring and SLO interpretation)

## Documentation goals and success criteria
Goals
- Make tier selection discoverable in the docs within 2 clicks from: Quickstart, Chat/Completions reference, and Configuration.
- Provide copy/paste examples for Python, TypeScript, and Go that reflect final request schema and naming.
- Reduce confusion between tier defaults vs explicit overrides (common support ticket pattern).
- Provide a “how to validate” section with clear steps and expected signals.

Success criteria (Docs)
- Customers can answer: “Which tier should I use for my route?” without contacting Support.
- Customers can answer: “What batching settings are actually applied?” using Console / explain endpoint / returned metadata.
- Support has a single canonical FAQ and migration guidance to link in tickets.

## Terminology and naming (customer-facing)
Canonical tier names (use consistently):
- Fast
- Standard
- Cost-efficient

In API/SDK/config, the wire representation is:
- `fast`
- `standard`
- `cost_efficient`

Do not introduce synonyms (“eco”, “balanced”) in customer docs.

## Proposed docs IA (information architecture)
Where content should live (docs site):
1) **Concepts**
   - New page: “Batching tiers (fast/standard/cost-efficient)”
2) **API Reference**
   - Update: Chat Completions request schema (add `batching_tier`)
   - Update: Completions request schema (add `batching_tier`)
   - Update: Embeddings request schema (tier supported or explicitly not supported; confirm final behavior during beta)
3) **Configuration / Performance**
   - Update: “Performance tuning” page to recommend tiers first; keep explicit knobs as advanced overrides
4) **Observability**
   - Update: “Latency & cost observability” to reference tier dashboards and what to monitor
5) **Deployments**
   - Update: Dedicated config guide (tier selection + per-route policy)
   - Update: Private (Helm/installer) configuration (values + migration notes)
6) **SDK Guides**
   - Update: Python / TypeScript / Go: include tier selection examples and typed enums
7) **Release Notes**
   - Link to the tier doc as the primary explainer; keep release note content minimal

## Content outline: new primary explainer page
Page title: “Batching tiers: choose your latency/cost profile”

Required sections
1) What batching tiers do
   - “A batching tier selects safe defaults for batching and queueing behavior based on workload signals.”
   - Call out that behavior is workload-aware but bounded by tier guardrails.

2) Tier recommendations (table)
Include a decision table customers can use quickly:
- Fast: lowest p95 latency / best streaming cadence; lowest batching; higher $/token
- Standard: balanced defaults; recommended for most interactive chat routes
- Cost-efficient: higher batching and queue delay; best $/token for non-urgent tasks; may increase tail latency and timeouts if your client timeout is too aggressive

3) Known constraints / best practices
- Streaming: prefer `fast` or `standard` for interactive UX; cost-efficient can reduce token cadence under load
- Tight client timeouts: avoid `cost_efficient` until you increase timeouts or confirm with canary
- Long-context / large prompts: may behave differently; link to “long-context considerations” subsection

4) How to configure
- API request examples (chat/completions)
- Console selection (once UI ships)
- Dedicated/Private config examples (YAML snippets)

5) Precedence rules (must be explicit)
- If customer sets explicit batching knobs, they override tier defaults.
- If no explicit batching knobs are set, tier determines defaults.
- If neither is set, platform default tier applies (during beta: likely `standard` for opt-in cohort; confirm per PRD).
- If an incompatible combination is provided, request fails validation with actionable error.

6) How to validate your effective config
- Use “effective config” / “explain” endpoint (or returned metadata headers) to confirm applied tier and resolved parameters.
- Link to dashboards and key metrics (p95, queue delay, batch size distribution, timeout/cancel rate).

7) Troubleshooting
- “I saw higher timeouts on cost-efficient”
- “Streaming feels choppy on fast/standard”
- “My overrides don’t seem to apply”

## API reference updates
### Request schema changes
Add `batching_tier` to relevant request bodies.

Example snippet (Chat Completions)
- Include a minimal example:
  - `model`
  - `messages`
  - `batching_tier: "standard"`

Also include an “advanced override” example showing `batching_tier` + explicit knobs, paired with a warning that explicit knobs win.

### Validation and error messages
Document expected validation errors:
- unsupported tier value
- tier not supported for route/model/region (during beta)
- illegal combinations (e.g., negative queue delay)

### Backwards compatibility
- Existing clients not sending `batching_tier` continue working.
- Existing explicit batching settings keep current behavior.

## SDK updates (examples + typing)
Owned by DevEx with SDK owners (Monica Patel coordinating).

Required updates
- Add examples for selecting `batching_tier` in:
  - Python SDK
  - TypeScript SDK
  - Go SDK (if supported; if not, update REST example)

Python example (docs site)
- Show `batching_tier="fast"` for interactive streaming chat.
- Show `batching_tier="cost_efficient"` for offline summarization.

TypeScript example
- Ensure enum/union types are correct: `"fast" | "standard" | "cost_efficient"`.

Go example
- If the SDK supports request structs, ensure field tag matches JSON name `batching_tier`.

Docstring references
- Each SDK should link to the canonical explainer page.

## Migration notes (customer-facing)
Add a dedicated “Migration: from manual batching knobs to tiers” section.

Include
- Who should migrate: customers with ad-hoc batching settings that were copied from old examples, or who want safer defaults.
- Who should not migrate yet: customers with highly tuned low-latency interactive workloads where existing overrides were proven in production and they cannot risk change.

Step-by-step migration procedure
1) Record current latency/cost metrics and client timeouts.
2) Confirm whether you have explicit batching knobs configured today.
3) Start by setting `batching_tier="standard"` on one low-risk route.
4) Do not remove overrides until you confirm tier outcomes; then remove overrides to fully adopt tier defaults.
5) Validate effective config and compare:
   - p50/p95 latency
   - time-to-first-token (streaming)
   - timeout/cancel rate
   - $/1M tokens (or $/token)
6) Expand rollout route-by-route.

Explicit call-outs
- Removing explicit knobs changes behavior; tiers may choose different queue delay / max batch settings depending on workload signals.
- If you need deterministic behavior, keep explicit overrides and document why.

## FAQ (customer-facing)
This FAQ should exist as a section on the explainer page and be linkable by Support.

Required questions
1) What’s the difference between `standard` and `cost_efficient`?
2) Will tiers change output quality?
   - Explain that batching can indirectly affect sampling timing in rare cases; Redwood uses quality gates and regression checks; recommend customers run prompt-set evals if they are extremely sensitive.
3) Are tiers available for streaming?
   - Yes, but guidance differs; call out token cadence sensitivity.
4) Can I set tiers per route?
   - Yes; recommend interactive routes use `standard` or `fast`, offline routes use `cost_efficient`.
5) Do tiers apply to Dedicated and Private?
   - Yes; include deployment notes and where to configure.
6) I set `batching_tier` and also set manual knobs—what happens?
   - Manual knobs override tier defaults; `batching_tier` still labels intent and fills in unset values.
7) How do I know what values were actually used?
   - Console effective config view, explain endpoint, and/or response metadata.
8) How does this interact with overload protection?
   - Cost-efficient tier may admit higher batching; overload protection still enforces safety; if load shedding occurs, you may see specific errors; link to error codes page if available.

## Observability and “how to validate” docs updates
Add a subsection in the latency/cost observability docs:
- “Monitoring tier behavior during rollout”

Metrics to mention (customer-level)
- Latency (p50/p95/p99)
- Queue delay (p95/p99) and batch wait time
- Batch size distribution
- GPU utilization (Dedicated/Private customers)
- Timeout/cancel rates

Practical checks
- For streaming: time-to-first-token and average token cadence under load
- For non-streaming: total request latency and tail

## Beta-specific documentation
During beta, we must clearly indicate:
- Supported models and regions (link to release notes / status page)
- How to opt in/out (feature flag / Console toggle / account setting)
- Known limitations (e.g., embeddings support, tool-calls edge cases, long-context behavior)

Add a prominent “Beta” callout block at the top of the explainer page.

## Ownership and execution plan
Owners
- Primary doc plan owner: Elliot Price
- SDK example coordination: Monica Patel
- Product review / messaging: Aditya Rao
- Hosted API schema review: Wei Chen
- SLO wording and metrics review: Sean Gallagher

Milestones (aligned to project phases)
- Phase 0–1: Draft explainer page + API reference deltas (DevEx + Product review)
- Phase 2: Add migration + FAQ + observability “validate” section; integrate Console screenshots once stable
- Phase 3: Beta release notes linking + SDK examples live; final terminology audit

## Review checklist (must pass before beta docs ship)
Content correctness
- Tier names and wire values consistent everywhere (`cost_efficient`, not `cost-efficient` in code).
- Precedence rules stated explicitly with at least one example.
- Streaming guidance is clear and not contradictory.
- Beta limitations clearly stated.

Technical accuracy
- Request schemas match actual API/SDK fields.
- Examples run end-to-end (validated by DevEx).
- “Effective config” instructions match shipped endpoint/Console.

Support readiness
- FAQ answers are specific and link to one canonical page.
- Migration procedure contains a safe staged rollout recommendation.

## Open questions / follow-ups
1) Final supported surfaces at beta: embeddings route support and any model-specific exclusions.
2) What is the default tier when customers do not specify `batching_tier`? (Product decision; document explicitly.)
3) Final name and format for “effective config” visibility: response headers vs explicit explain endpoint vs both.
4) Whether to document recommended client timeout minimums per tier (strongly recommended for cost-efficient).

## Appendix: Draft examples (placeholders until final API is confirmed)
### REST (Chat Completions)
- Include in final docs once schema is finalized:
  - POST /v1/chat/completions
  - { model, messages, batching_tier }

### SDK example scenarios
- Interactive support chat (streaming): `fast`
- Product Q&A in-app: `standard`
- Offline summarization / batch processing: `cost_efficient`

(These examples should be duplicated in Python/TS/Go with identical scenario naming to reduce confusion across languages.)
